title: Extremal laws for coupon collection with group drawings
shortTitle: How slow, and how fast, can group coupon collection be?
oneLine: Steiner designs are the slowest fair laws, a fair law with large packages is less than one draw slower than uniform sampling on average, and partitions are the fastest.
abstract: A collector wants a full set of n different coupons, but each box holds a group of s of them, and whoever fills the boxes decides how the groups overlap. How quickly can a full set be completed, and how slowly can completion be made while staying fair, with every coupon equally common? Grunbaum and Yaakobi conjectured that drawing uniformly from all groups (the full model) is the slowest fair rule; Barak-Pelleg and Berend disproved this with the Fano plane and asked how slow a fair rule can be and how large the excess over the full model can become. Fang and Chang conjectured that equal disjoint groups are fastest whenever s divides n. This candidate shows that when the omitted coupons can form a Steiner 2-design, sampling it is the slowest fair rule after every number of draws, and only the design does this; seven coupons in boxes of four take 47/12 boxes on average against 257/68 for the full model. In every critical window, where λ is the expected number of coupons still missing after k boxes, the slowest fair mean is k + min(1, λ) + o(1), against k + 1 − e^(−λ) for the full model, for every population size. No fair rule is more than 1/e + (1 − γ)/ln(n/r) boxes slower on average than the full model, where r = n − s: less than one box whenever boxes hold at least half the coupons, with limit 1/e attained. An exhaustive exact search of all small cases shows that the Fano plane is the slowest fair rule at Barak-Pelleg and Berend's own example and that six coupons in boxes of three is the smallest case where the full model is not slowest. On the fast side, every rule needs at least max{xH(x), 1 + x} boxes on average with x = n/s; equal disjoint groups are uniquely fastest when s divides n, proving the Fang–Chang conjecture, and complementary partitions when n − s divides n. Barak-Pelleg and Berend's star mechanism already reaches k + 1 in its own windows; the h = 1 product bound is Pelekis, Ramon and Wang's Theorem 2.6 after Poissonisation; Berend and Sher introduced the complementary law and computed its mean. Limits: the critical-window result is asymptotic, converges slowly and uses an existential construction; several finite cases remain open. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Theorem 3.1 (proof): for every balanced law, Pr(T > j) ≤ npʲ − (n(n−1)/r)uʲ with u = r(r−1)/(n(n−1)); equality at any j ≥ 2 holds exactly for the uniform law on the blocks of a Steiner system S(2,r,n) as omitted sets, which is the slowest fair law in mean (seven coupons, boxes of four: 47/12 against 257/68).

Theorem 4.1 (proof): if npᵏ → λ ∈ (0,∞) for fixed k ≥ 2, the largest mean over fair laws is k + min{1, λ} + o(1), against k + 1 − e^(−λ) + o(1) for the full model; the asymptotic excess peaks at 1/e when λ = 1. Barak-Pelleg and Berend's star mechanism already attains k + 1 in its windows (λ > 1).
Theorem 5.4 (proof): every fair law has mean at most 1/e + (1 − γ)/ln(n/r) above the full model, for all n and r; this is at most 0.978 when r ≤ n/2, and the limit 1/e is attained.

Proposition 6.1 (computer-assisted, exact): for n ≤ 7 and for n = 8 with s ∈ {2, 6}, the full model is the unique slowest fair mechanism except at (6,3), (7,3) and (7,4); at (7,3) the Fano plane attains the maximum 163/30 among 2,505,121 fair mechanisms, and (6,3) is the smallest counterexample to Grunbaum and Yaakobi's Conjecture 2.

Theorems 7.2 and 7.3 (proof): every law on packages of size at most s has E T ≥ xHₓ with x = n/s, with equality exactly for a uniform partition when s divides n; this proves the Fang–Chang conjecture with uniqueness. The h = 1 product bound is Pelekis, Ramon and Wang's Theorem 2.6 after Poissonisation.

Theorem 7.5 (proof): every such law has E T ≥ 1 + n/s, with equality among laws on packages of exactly s coupons only for the uniform law on a partition of the omitted sets when (n − s) divides n; the law and its mean are due to Berend and Sher.

narration:
Imagine collecting a full set of stickers when every packet holds a group of them, and whoever fills the packets decides how the groups overlap. How quickly can a full set be finished, and how slowly can it be made while staying fair, with every sticker equally common? The same question arises when DNA reads arrive in batches, when computers contact random groups of servers, and when copies of data are spread across machines.

Earlier work conjectured that drawing uniformly from all possible groups is the slowest fair rule. That conjecture was disproved with a small geometry called the Fano plane, which left open how slow a fair rule can really be. On the fast side, it was conjectured that splitting the stickers into equal separate groups is always quickest.

This release answers several of these questions. When the stickers left out of each packet can form a special pattern called a Steiner design, sampling that pattern is the slowest fair rule after any number of packets, and only the design does this. For collections of every size, the slowest fair rule is also found in a family of critical cases, up to an error that fades as collections grow. And no fair rule is ever much slower than uniform sampling. When each packet holds at least half the stickers, the extra wait is less than one packet on average, and as packets come to hold almost everything it approaches a little over a third of a packet, a limit that is actually reached.

An exact computer search of every small case shows that the Fano plane is the slowest fair rule in its own example, and that six stickers in packets of three is the smallest case where uniform sampling is not the slowest. On the fast side, the release proves that equal separate groups are the unique fastest rule whenever the packet size divides the number of stickers, which settles that conjecture.

The idea is simple. Every fair rule leaves the same expected number of stickers missing; slow rules make them turn up one at a time, and fast rules make them vanish in clumps.

There are limits. The critical-case results describe large collections and settle in slowly, the exact slowest rule without a design is known only for small collections, and the fastest rule remains open in the remaining cases. Earlier work already reached the slowest value in some critical cases and supplied one key inequality, and the paper credits both. This is an unrefereed candidate, checked by internal AI-assisted review and exact computer checks rather than by external experts.

decisionObject.description: Decide how slow or fast group sampling of a population can make complete coverage while every item stays equally likely, and which designs to use or benchmark against when building sampling, coverage or quorum schemes.
decisionObject.scope: Independent draws of packages of s out of n items; fair laws (equal item frequencies) on the slow side and arbitrary laws on packages of size at most s on the fast side; exact finite results, asymptotic critical windows and exhaustive small cases.
